claims.text: The target material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The intended initial specimens have less than 0.1 wt.% oxygen and minimal extrinsic defects.
The new approach separately models lattice thermal conductivity and electronic thermal transport.
The approach incorporates detailed phonon dispersion, explicit anharmonicity, disorder-induced phonon localization, and oxygen-dependent defect scattering.
The new approach will reduce the mean absolute error of lattice thermal-conductivity predictions by about 20% relative to earlier Debye-temperature-based approaches.
Local lattice distortions and compositional disorder enhance phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortions and compositional disorder do not significantly alter electronic transport pathways.
Temperature-dependent anharmonic scattering and chemical-disorder effects modify phonon lifetimes.
Separating lattice and electronic transport avoids conflation attributed to earlier bulk Debye approximations.
Earlier analytical methods were based on perfect, defect-free crystals and did not account adequately for local disorder or oxygen-induced scattering.
Earlier methods typically show larger deviations from experimental total thermal conductivity than the proposed approach.
An oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr specimen has a reported total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m).
Below approximately 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are of similar magnitude.
An isolated lattice-conductivity prediction should diverge from measured total conductivity below approximately 200 K.
The model is applicable to high-purity, defect-controlled HfNbTaTiZr between 300 and 1200 K.
Predictions of the isolated lattice contribution become less reliable below approximately 200 K.
Significant oxygen or other defects may introduce scattering mechanisms beyond those represented by the model.
A comparison of samples containing less than 0.1 wt.% oxygen and approximately 1 wt.% oxygen can test the model's treatment of defect scattering.
A lattice-conductivity discrepancy greater than 20% or an inconsistent temperature dependence would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The approach is said to incorporate oxygen-dependent defect scattering, but significant oxygen is also placed beyond its reliable scope, while the proposed validation nevertheless applies it to a specimen with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen. The modeled oxygen range is not defined, so it is unclear whether this decisive test is inside or outside the claimed applicability domain.
